power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 30 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  0 of 82 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 82 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (30 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``DOI``, ``OpenAlexID``, ``PAPER_LINK`` while the data has `PAPER_LINK`, `YEAR_PUBLISHED`, `PAPER_TITLE`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 82 data columns across 2 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (30 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``DOI``, ``OpenAlexID``, ``PAPER_LINK`` while the data has `PAPER_LINK`, `YEAR_PUBLISHED`, `PAPER_TITLE`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 82 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("Analysis Code/Results.xlsx", "Analysis Code/Results.xlsx", "Analysis Code/Results.xlsx", "Analysis Code/Results.xlsx", "Database/Results.xlsx", "Database/Results.xlsx", "Database/Results.xlsx", "Database/Results.xlsx" ), Column = c("ANALYSIS_CODE_FORMAT", "OSF_ID", "PAPER_TITLE", "SHARING_LINK", "ANALYSIS_CODE_FORMAT", "OSF_ID", "PAPER_TITLE", "SHARING_LINK"), Issues = c("🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: R, Python/R, python", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: JQ56S/jq56s", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 90 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: http://OSF", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: R, Python/R, python", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: JQ56S/jq56s", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 90 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: http://OSF" )), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: In the wake of psychology's credibility revolution, open science practices such as data sharing have become more prevalent, yet researchers often cite a lack of professional incentives as a barrier to adoption.
This report examines the association between data sharing and scholarly impact in visual search and eye-movement literature, building on the systematic audit by Godwin et al. (2025).
text.formatted: This report examines the association between data sharing and scholarly impact in visual search and eye-movement literature, building on the systematic audit by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: I extended their dataset with bibliometric metadata from the OpenAlex registry and compared field-normalized, accumulated, and time-resolved citation impact between articles that did and did not share data.

Although articles that shared data showed a small citation advantage in unadjusted analyses, this difference was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for publication characteristics such as publication age and journal citedness.
A time-resolved analysis revealed a small association between sharing status and the trajectory of citation accrual, but did not establish a robust early citation advantage.
Citation impact also did not differ by data granularity: sharing fine-grained fixation-level data did not confer greater benefit than sharing coarser participant-level summaries.
These observational findings provide no robust evidence of an overall citation advantage associated with data sharing in this research domain, nor of an additional advantage for finer-grained data.
They do not establish that data sharing has no citation benefit, but highlight the importance of examining how its association with scholarly impact varies across research contexts and over time.

In the aftermath of the "replication crisis" in psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015; Baker, 2016), many researchers have adopted more rigorous and transparent practices, ushering in a "credibility revolution" (Korbmacher et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the aftermath of the "replication crisis" in psychology <ref type="bibr">(Open Science Collaboration, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baker, 2016)</ref>, many researchers have adopted more rigorous and transparent practices, ushering in a "credibility revolution" <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Korbmacher et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the adoption of open science practices has been uneven.

While the disclosure of funding sources and conflicts of interest is now common practice, the sharing of code, experimental materials, and data remains relatively rare across psychological research (Hardwicke et al., 2022; Hardwicke et al., 2024).
text.formatted: While the disclosure of funding sources and conflicts of interest is now common practice, the sharing of code, experimental materials, and data remains relatively rare across psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hardwicke et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hardwicke et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These broad findings primarily characterize the general state of the field, while more recent work has shifted toward examining open science practices within more circumscribed contexts, including specific subfields (Rochios & Richmond, 2024), journals (Laurinavichyute et al., 2022), and psychological phenomena (Wiechert et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These broad findings primarily characterize the general state of the field, while more recent work has shifted toward examining open science practices within more circumscribed contexts, including specific subfields <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Rochios & Richmond, 2024)</ref>, journals <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Laurinavichyute et al., 2022)</ref>, and psychological phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wiechert et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this line of work, Godwin et al. (2025) systematically reviewed data-, code-, and materials-sharing practices in the visual search and eye-movement domain.
text.formatted: Building on this line of work, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref> systematically reviewed data-, code-, and materials-sharing practices in the visual search and eye-movement domain.

text.text: Surveying 260 research outputs, comprising both peer-reviewed articles and OSF repositories published between 2017 and 2022, they found that approximately one third of journal articles reported sharing at least one research output.

When sharing occurred, it most often involved data: over 90% of sharing articles made datasets available, whereas other outputs (e.g., analysis code or experimental materials) were less consistently shared.

Importantly, Godwin et al. further distinguished shared datasets by their level of granularity, differentiating between fixation-level data, triallevel aggregates, and participant-level summaries. Godwin et al. (2025) provided an important benchmark for the state of sharing in visual search research, and even developed the "Find It, Access It, Reuse It" scorecard to assist researchers in publishing reusable data.
text.formatted: Importantly, Godwin et al. further distinguished shared datasets by their level of granularity, differentiating between fixation-level data, triallevel aggregates, and participant-level summaries. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref> provided an important benchmark for the state of sharing in visual search research, and even developed the "Find It, Access It, Reuse It" scorecard to assist researchers in publishing reusable data.

text.text: However, their evaluation left a fundamental question unexamined: whether data sharing is associated with greater scholarly impact for authors.
That is, does the scientific community, and visual search researchers in particular, "reward" scientists who share their data through increased citation impact?
Several previous studies have examined the relationship between data sharing and citation impact.

In their seminal work, Piwowar et al. (2007) demonstrated an "Open Data Citation Advantage" (ODCA) among 85 cancer microarray clinical trial publications: they showed that data sharing was associated with 69% more citations, after adjusting for journal impact factor, publication date, and U.S.-affiliated authorship.
text.formatted: In their seminal work, <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Piwowar et al. (2007)</ref> demonstrated an "Open Data Citation Advantage" (ODCA) among 85 cancer microarray clinical trial publications: they showed that data sharing was associated with 69% more citations, after adjusting for journal impact factor, publication date, and U.S.-affiliated authorship.

text.text: In a subsequent large-scale analysis of 10,000 molecular biology articles, Piwowar and Vision (2013) reported a 5-13% ODCA, while controlling for publication date, authorship, and institutional factors. Christensen et al. (2019) estimated an increase of 97-109 accumulated citations for articles in political science and economics that shared their data, although they raised concerns about the causal interpretation of this estimate.
text.formatted: In a subsequent large-scale analysis of 10,000 molecular biology articles, <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Piwowar and Vision (2013)</ref> reported a 5-13% ODCA, while controlling for publication date, authorship, and institutional factors. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Christensen et al. (2019)</ref> estimated an increase of 97-109 accumulated citations for articles in political science and economics that shared their data, although they raised concerns about the causal interpretation of this estimate.

text.text: At a larger scale, Colavizza et al. (2020) reported a roughly 25% citation advantage within the first three years post-publication for articles that included a link to shared data, and Colavizza et al. (2024) estimated a smaller long-term advantage of approximately 4.3% in total citation accumulation, while controlling for multiple publication features (e.g., publication age and field).
text.formatted: At a larger scale, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Colavizza et al. (2020)</ref> reported a roughly 25% citation advantage within the first three years post-publication for articles that included a link to shared data, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Colavizza et al. (2024)</ref> estimated a smaller long-term advantage of approximately 4.3% in total citation accumulation, while controlling for multiple publication features (e.g., publication age and field).

text.text: OpenAlex, an open scholarly metadata database (Priem et al., 2022).
text.formatted: OpenAlex, an open scholarly metadata database <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Priem et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Recent benchmarking analyses found that OpenAlex's coverage is comparable to that of proprietary databases such as Web of Science and Scopus (Alperin et al., 2024; Culbert et al., 2025), and that OpenAlex may provide more complete citation-count records (Thelwall & Jiang, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent benchmarking analyses found that OpenAlex's coverage is comparable to that of proprietary databases such as Web of Science and Scopus <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Alperin et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Culbert et al., 2025)</ref>, and that OpenAlex may provide more complete citation-count records <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Thelwall & Jiang, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Using field-normalized and time-resolved citation measures, I examined whether data sharing is associated with higher citation impact, while accounting for publication characteristics previously considered in bibliometric research, including publication age, journal citedness, and preprint availability (e.g., Piwowar et al., 2007; Tahamtan et al., 2016; Abramo et al., 2023; Colavizza et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Using field-normalized and time-resolved citation measures, I examined whether data sharing is associated with higher citation impact, while accounting for publication characteristics previously considered in bibliometric research, including publication age, journal citedness, and preprint availability (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Piwowar et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tahamtan et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Abramo et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Colavizza et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: I hypothesized that articles that share data would exhibit greater citation impact than those that do not.

In addition, building on Godwin et al.'s argument that finer-grained data can facilitate replication and secondary analyses, I hypothesized that articles sharing finer-grained data would be associated with a greater citation advantage than articles sharing coarse, aggregated data.
I analyzed the corpus of publications curated by Godwin et al. (2025).
text.formatted: I analyzed the corpus of publications curated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: Following their inclusion criteria, I selected studies published between 2017 and 2022 that involved human participants and used visual search and eye-movement analysis.
Records lacking a valid article title or link were excluded, resulting in an initial pool of 𝑁 = 251 publications.
Bibliometric metadata were retrieved by querying the OpenAlex API using its Python wrapper, pyAlex 1 .
Articles were matched using available DOIs, URLs, or titles.
Of the 251 queried records, 11 queries were unsuccessful, and an additional 6 returned duplicate DOIs.
The final analytic sample comprised 𝑁 = 234 articles.
All metadata were queried on September 2, 2026.
Because OpenAlex continuously updates its database, all metrics represent a snapshot at this date.
The OpenAlex records for all analyzed articles had been updated within the three weeks preceding data extraction.

A two one-sided tests procedure for equivalence (TOST; Lakens, 2017) indicated that record-update dates for sharing and non-sharing articles were equivalent within a prespecified ±7-day margin (𝑝 < 0.001).
text.formatted: A two one-sided tests procedure for equivalence (TOST; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Lakens, 2017)</ref> indicated that record-update dates for sharing and non-sharing articles were equivalent within a prespecified ±7-day margin (𝑝 < 0.001).

text.text: This provides evidence against biases in citation impact due to unbalanced record-update timing (see Supplementary S1).
Using the annotations provided by Godwin et al. (2025), articles were classified according to the granularity of shared data: fixation-level, trial-level, participant-level, or no data shared.
text.formatted: Using the annotations provided by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref>, articles were classified according to the granularity of shared data: fixation-level, trial-level, participant-level, or no data shared.

text.text: Articles that shared data at multiple levels were classified according to the finest available granularity (e.g., articles sharing both fixation-and participant-level data were classified as fixation-level; see Supplementary S2
text.formatted: Articles that shared data at multiple levels were classified according to the finest available granularity (e.g., articles sharing both fixation-and participant-level data were classified as fixation-level; see Supplementary <ref type="table">S2</ref>

text.text: For each article, I retrieved the total citation count and annual citation history from OpenAlex.

I also retrieved each article's Field-Weighted Citation Impact (FWCI; ) 2 , a 1 pyAlex is available via the Python Package Index: https://pypi.org/project/pyalex/ 2 More information on how OpenAlex calculates the FWCI metric can be found here: https://help.openalex.org/hc/en-us/articles/24735753007895-Field-Weighted-Citation-Impact-FWCI Snowball Metricfoot_0 that quantifies citation performance relative to publications from the same field and publication year (Colledge, 2014; Dresbeck, 2015).
text.formatted: I also retrieved each article's Field-Weighted Citation Impact (FWCI; ) 2 , a 1 pyAlex is available via the Python Package Index: <ref type="url" target="https://pypi.org/project/pyalex/">https://pypi.org/project/pyalex/</ref> 2 More information on how OpenAlex calculates the FWCI metric can be found here: <ref type="url" target="https://help.openalex.org/hc/en-us/articles/24735753007895-Field-Weighted-Citation-Impact-FWCI">https://help.openalex.org/hc/en-us/articles/24735753007895-Field-Weighted-Citation-Impact-FWCI</ref> Snowball Metric<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> that quantifies citation performance relative to publications from the same field and publication year <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Colledge, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Dresbeck, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: I prioritized FWCI over the ℎ-index (Hirsch, 2005) because the latter is confounded by the total number of publications and lacks sensitivity to field-specific citation densities and researcher career length (Bornmann & Daniel, 2007; Iglesias & Pecharromán, 2007).
text.formatted: I prioritized FWCI over the ℎ-index <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hirsch, 2005)</ref> because the latter is confounded by the total number of publications and lacks sensitivity to field-specific citation densities and researcher career length <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bornmann & Daniel, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Iglesias & Pecharromán, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Following previous bibliometric analyses (e.g., Piwowar et al., 2007; Piwowar & Vision, 2013; Tahamtan et al., 2016), I included several article-level covariates in the regression models to account for potential confounding.
text.formatted: Following previous bibliometric analyses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Piwowar et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Piwowar & Vision, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tahamtan et al., 2016)</ref>, I included several article-level covariates in the regression models to account for potential confounding.

text.text: These included publication age, preprint availability, journal two-year mean citedness, open access status, number of authors, U.S. institutional affiliation (at least one author affiliated with a U.S. institution; 99 articles, 42.3%).
In their original dataset, Godwin et al. (2025) used a categorical "Year Published" field to enforce their 2017-2022 inclusion window.
text.formatted: In their original dataset, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref> used a categorical "Year Published" field to enforce their 2017-2022 inclusion window.

text.text: However, articles sometimes appear online before formal issue publication, resulting in an earlier de facto publication date (Haustein et al., 2015).
text.formatted: However, articles sometimes appear online before formal issue publication, resulting in an earlier de facto publication date <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Haustein et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: To capture citation exposure more precisely, I used OpenAlex's "Publication Date" field, which attempts to record the earliest available date of electronic publicationfoot_1.
text.formatted: To capture citation exposure more precisely, I used OpenAlex's "Publication Date" field, which attempts to record the earliest available date of electronic publication<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref>.

text.text: In 10 cases, articles recorded by Godwin et al. (2025) as published in 2017 or 2018 were indexed by OpenAlex as published in 2016.
text.formatted: In 10 cases, articles recorded by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref> as published in 2017 or 2018 were indexed by OpenAlex as published in 2016.

text.text: To preserve consistency with the original curation, these articles were retained in the sample.

For all regression and timeresolved analyses, however, article age was measured as the number of weeks from the OpenAlex publication date to December 31, 2025, providing a continuous measure of exposure time for citation accumulation.

Because official Journal Impact Factor data (JIF; Garfield, 1995) are proprietary to Clarivate 5 , I used OpenAlex's "Two-Year Mean Citedness" as a publicly available alternative (see Supplementary S3).
text.formatted: Because official Journal Impact Factor data (JIF; <ref type="bibr">Garfield, 1995)</ref> are proprietary to Clarivate 5 , I used OpenAlex's "Two-Year Mean Citedness" as a publicly available alternative (see Supplementary <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S3</ref>).

text.text: This proxy was shown to correlate highly with official JIF rankings (Spearman's 𝑟 = 0.94-0.96; Perianes-Rodríguez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This proxy was shown to correlate highly with official JIF rankings (Spearman's 𝑟 = 0.94-0.96; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Perianes-Rodríguez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, because OpenAlex does not provide historical journal-level metrics, the values used here reflect current journal citedness rather than the impact metric available when each article was published.

To determine whether an article had an associated preprint, I checked whether the article's OpenAlex record included commonly used preprint servers (e.g., OSF, bioRxiv) as an associated publication venue.
This identified 28 articles linked to a preprint.
To complement this, I queried CrossRef -a foundational, publicly available, metadata infrastructure (Hendricks et al., 2020) -which identified 11 additional preprints.
text.formatted: To complement this, I queried CrossRef -a foundational, publicly available, metadata infrastructure <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hendricks et al., 2020</ref>) -which identified 11 additional preprints.

text.text: Finally, an automated search of major preprint repositories for the remaining articles identified 8 additional preprints.
Candidate matches were accepted only when the titles were highly similar, the first and last authors matched exactly, and the preprint posting year preceded or matched the journal publication year.
In total, 47 articles were matched to a preprint (20.1%).
This estimate is likely conservative, as incomplete metadata and imperfect retrieval may have left some preprints undetected.

Although open access (OA) can be defined in several ways (Piwowar et al., 2018), OpenAlex uses a broad definition: a publication is classified as OA if a free, openly accessible full-text version is available, including through journals, authors' websites, or preprint servers.
text.formatted: Although open access (OA) can be defined in several ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Piwowar et al., 2018)</ref>, OpenAlex uses a broad definition: a publication is classified as OA if a free, openly accessible full-text version is available, including through journals, authors' websites, or preprint servers.

text.text: In the present dataset, 199 articles (85.0%) were classified as OA. 𝜒 2test of independence found no evidence of an association between OA status and preprint availability (𝜒 2 (1) = 0.0002, 𝑝 = 0.99).
All analyses were conducted in Python 3.14 and R 4.5.2.
Statistical significance was set a priori at 𝛼 = 0.05.
Tests of the association between data sharing and citation impact were directional (one-sided), reflecting the hypothesis that data sharing is associated with higher citation impact.
When applicable, 𝑝-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the false-discovery rate procedure (FDR; Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: When applicable, 𝑝-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the false-discovery rate procedure (FDR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: To address skewness and improve the suitability with statistical model assumptions, several article characteristics were transformed prior to model fitting.
Citation counts were strongly right-skewed (𝑔1 = 1.96), approximately power-law distributed (Clauset et al., 2009), and accumulated over time.
text.formatted: Citation counts were strongly right-skewed (𝑔1 = 1.96), approximately power-law distributed <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Clauset et al., 2009)</ref>, and accumulated over time.

text.text: Accordingly, both citation counts and article age were entered on the 𝑙𝑜𝑔 scale to linearize their relationship.
Furthermore, to accommodate uncited articles, citation counts were transformed as log(citations + 1) (Thelwall & Wilson, 2014).
text.formatted: Furthermore, to accommodate uncited articles, citation counts were transformed as log(citations + 1) <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Thelwall & Wilson, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Author counts were also 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformed, substantially reducing their skewness (from 𝑔1 = 1.39 to 𝑔1 = 0.14).
Conversely, journal two-year mean citedness, although right-skewed, was retained on its original scale because 𝑙𝑜𝑔transformation over-corrected its skewness (from 𝑔1 = 0.38 to 𝑔1 = -0.97).

FWCI scores were processed according to the imputation strategy proposed by Dengler (2024): the five articles with FWCI = 0 were assigned half the minimum non-zero FWCI value within the same publication year, after which all FWCI scores were 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformed (reducing skew from 𝑔1 = 1.44 to 𝑔1 = -0.47).

text.text: To assess feature independence and potential multicollinearity, I examined pairwise correlations and calculated variance inflation factors (VIF; Fox & Monette, 1992).
text.formatted: To assess feature independence and potential multicollinearity, I examined pairwise correlations and calculated variance inflation factors <ref type="bibr">(VIF;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fox & Monette, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Pairwise correlations were modest (all pairwise |𝑟 𝑖,𝑗 | ≤ 0.29), and VIFs were low (all 𝑉𝐼𝐹 𝑖 ≤ 1.2; see Supplementary S4), indicating no substantial multicollinearity among the predictors (O'Brien, 2007).
Because nonsignificant results alone do not establish the absence of an effect, null findings were followed up with two procedures.
First, two one-sided tests (TOST; Lakens, 2017) assessed equivalence within a smallest effect size of interest of ±0.3 on the 𝑙𝑜𝑔 scale, corresponding to differences of -26% to +35%.
text.formatted: First, two one-sided tests (TOST; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Lakens, 2017)</ref> assessed equivalence within a smallest effect size of interest of ±0.3 on the 𝑙𝑜𝑔 scale, corresponding to differences of -26% to +35%.

text.text: Notably, a margin tight enough to exclude previously reported citation premiums (approximately 4% to 25%) cannot be resolved using the current sample size.

Second, Bayes factors (𝐵𝐹s) were calculated from each model coefficient and its standard error (bayesplay v0.9.3; Dienes, 2014; Colling, 2023), comparing a point-null hypothesis (ℋ 0 : 𝑏 = 0) with an alternative hypothesis (ℋ 1 ) using a zero-centred normal prior with 𝑆𝐷 = 0.3, matching the equivalence margin.

text.text: To assess sensitivity to this prior, 𝐵𝐹s were recalculated using prior 𝑆𝐷 = 0.15, 0.6; the direction of evidence was unchanged.

To characterize article-level covariates before modelling citation impact, I examined the associations between data-sharing status and six article characteristics: presence of a U.S.-affiliated author, open-access status, links to an associated preprint, publication age, number of authors, and venue two-year mean citedness.

Binary characteristics were compared using chi-squared tests of independence (McHugh, 2013), and continuous characteristics using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (Mann & Whitney, 1947). 𝑝-values across all six comparisons were corrected using the FDR procedure.

text.text: Articles that shared data were published in venues with significantly higher two-year mean citedness, had 4.3 times higher odds of having an associated preprint, and were more recently published (all adjusted 𝑝 𝑠 ≤ 0.01).
The groups did not differ significantly in number of authors, U.S. authorship, or open-access status (all adjusted 𝑝 𝑠 ≥ 0.08; see detailed results in Table 1 and Figure 1).

text.text: I then fitted a linear mixed-effects (LME) model to evaluate the association between data sharing and citation counts, while controlling for the six other article characteristics and including a random intercept grouped by publication venue.
Data-sharing status was not significantly associated with accumulated citations (𝑏 = 0.04, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.13, 𝑧 = 0.29, 𝑝 = 0.77).

The Bayes factor provided only anecdotal evidence for the absence of an effect (𝐵𝐹 ℋ 0 ℋ 1 ⁄ = 2.4), whereas TOST supported equivalence within a ±0.3 difference on the 𝑙𝑜𝑔 scale (𝑝 = 0.02, 90% CI: [-0.18, 0.25]), constraining the plausible difference to between -16% and +29%.
Citation counts were significantly associated with publication age (𝑏 = 1.12, 𝑝 < 0.001) and the journal's two-year mean citedness (𝑏 = 0.18, 𝑝 = 0.013; see Table 3 and Figure 2).

text.text: In this adjusted model, the association between data-sharing status and FWCI was no longer statistically significant (𝑏 = 0.07, 𝑆𝐸 = 0.15, 𝑧 = 0.43, 𝑝 = 0.67), in contrast to the univariate comparison above.

text.text: (4) Citation Dynamics
To examine how citation accrual varied over time, I analyzed each article's annual citation counts in every calendar year post-publication (YPP).
Citations from the publication year ("Year 0") and the current incomplete year (2026) were excluded to avoid partial-year artifacts.

I fitted a linear mixed-effects (LME) model predicting 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformed annual citation counts (log(1 + Annual Citations)) from data-sharing status, YPP, and the article-level characteristics including in the preceding models: U.S.-affiliated authorship, open access, preprint availability, publication age, number of authors, and venue two-year mean citedness).
To capture the nonlinear temporal pattern of citation accrual, the model included a linear and a 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformed YPP term, both 𝑧-standardized.
The Sharing × YPP interaction tested whether citation trajectories differed between articles that shared data and those that did not.

To account for repeated annual observations within articles and the clustering of articles within venues, the model included random intercepts for venue and article nested within venue, as well as a random slope for YPP across articles.

Using Wilkinson-Rogers (1973) notation, the model was specified as follows: log(1 + Annual Citations) ~ 1 + 𝐶(Is Sharing) * 𝑧(YPP) + 𝑧(log(YPP)) + 𝐶(Is OA) + 𝐶(Has U.S. Author) + 𝐶(Has Preprint) + log(Publication Age) + log(Number of Authors) + Journal 2Y Mean Citedness + (1 | 𝐽𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑛𝑎𝑙) + (1 + YPP | 𝐽𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑛𝑎𝑙: 𝐴𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑙𝑒)

The model showed significant effects of venue two-year mean citedness (𝑏 = 0.12, 𝑝 = 0.01), the linear YPP term (𝑏 = -0.21, 𝑝 < 0.001), and the 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformed YPP term (𝑏 = 0.22, 𝑝 < 0.001), but no significant main effect of sharing status (𝑏 = 0.01, 𝑝 = 0.91; see Table 5 and Figure 3).
text.formatted: The model showed significant effects of venue two-year mean citedness (𝑏 = 0.12, 𝑝 = 0.01), the linear YPP term (𝑏 = -0.21, 𝑝 < 0.001), and the 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformed YPP term (𝑏 = 0.22, 𝑝 < 0.001), but no significant main effect of sharing status (𝑏 = 0.01, 𝑝 = 0.91; see Table <ref type="table">5</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>).

text.text: The interaction between sharing and YPP was statistically significant but small (𝑏 = -0.09 per SD of YPP, 95% CI [-0.17, -0.02], 𝑝 = 0.02): an estimated 4.5% (95% CI [0.8%, 8.0%]) multiplicative decrease in the ratio between sharing and non-sharing articles, for every additional year.

The interaction remained significant across several robustness checks, including an alternative distribution family (Poisson), alternative YPP specifications (quadratic and linear-only), and alternative constants in the 𝑙𝑜𝑔-transformation (log(𝑐 + Annual Citations) with 𝑐 = 0.5, 0.1).
Detailed results and robustness checks are available online at https://github.com/JonNir1/eye_movement_data_sharing.

text.text: As an exploratory follow-up, I compared citation accrued during the first full postpublication year ("Year 1").
The unadjusted comparison showed significantly higher citation counts among articles that shared data (𝑈 = 7482.5, one-sided 𝑝 = 0.003, 𝑟 𝑟𝑏 = 0.21, 𝐶𝐿𝐸𝑆 = 0.61).

However, the adjusted model estimated a smaller, statistically non-significant difference between the groups (predicted Δ = 0.13 on the log(1 + Annual Citations) scale, corresponding to an estimated 14% difference; 95% CI [-6%, 38%], 𝑝 = 0.18).
A comparison of cumulative citations over Years 1-3 yielded a similar pattern (results are available online).
Finally, I fitted a similarly specified model to the subset of data-sharing articles, to examine the differences among sharing-granularity classes over time.
Venue two-year mean citedness (𝑏 = 0.12, 𝑝 = 0.04) and the linear YPP term (𝑏 = -0.24, 𝑝 = 0.02) again showed significant effects.
U.S.-affiliation was also significant (𝑏 = 0.33, 𝑝 = 0.02), whereas the interaction between sharing class and YPP was not significant (all pairwise contrasts had FDR-corrected 𝑝 ≥ 0.3).

text.text: This report examined whether data sharing in visual search and eye-movement research is associated with greater citation impact, extending the descriptive audit of sharing practices reported by Godwin et al. (2025) with bibliometric indicators derived from OpenAlex.
text.formatted: This report examined whether data sharing in visual search and eye-movement research is associated with greater citation impact, extending the descriptive audit of sharing practices reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref> with bibliometric indicators derived from OpenAlex.

text.text: Contrary to my first hypothesis, the results revealed no robust evidence for a citation advantage among articles that shared data.

While initial univariate comparisons indicated a significantly higher Field-Weighted Citation Impact (FWCI) for sharing articles, this difference was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for publication characteristics.

Furthermore, contrary to my second hypothesis, I found no evidence that sharing finer-grained data (e.g., fixation-level data) was associated with greater citation impact than sharing coarser, aggregated summaries.
Previous bibliometric analyses have reported citation advantages associated with data sharing.
Yet support for this "Open Data Citation Advantage" (ODCA) stems mostly from massive aggregation, sometimes across multiple disciplines.

Analyses spanning molecular biology (Piwowar & Vision, 2013), political science and economics (Christensen et al., 2019), psychology (Pan et al., 2026), and large-scale, multidisciplinary corpora (Colavizza et al., 2020; Colavizza et al., 2024), consistently report citation premiums ranging from 4% to 25% for data-sharing articles, depending on statistical controls and the analyzed citation period.
text.formatted: Analyses spanning molecular biology <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Piwowar & Vision, 2013)</ref>, political science and economics <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Christensen et al., 2019)</ref>, psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Pan et al., 2026)</ref>, and large-scale, multidisciplinary corpora <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Colavizza et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Colavizza et al., 2024)</ref>, consistently report citation premiums ranging from 4% to 25% for data-sharing articles, depending on statistical controls and the analyzed citation period.

text.text: Large-scale, however, bibliometric studies necessarily aggregate across heterogeneous research communities.

Recent meta-scientific efforts complement this approach by examining Open Science practices within well-defined subfields, including specific psychological domains (e.g., Wiechert et al., 2024; Rochios & Richmond, 2024; Godwin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent meta-scientific efforts complement this approach by examining Open Science practices within well-defined subfields, including specific psychological domains (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Wiechert et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Rochios & Richmond, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present study adds to this literature by examining the ODCA within a specific research domain: in visual search and eye-movement research, there was no evidence for a citation advantage associated with data sharing.
These findings also speak to an ongoing debate regarding researchers' incentives to adopt Open Science practices.

Although acceptance of Open Science principles has increased (e.g., Korbmacher et al., 2023), some researchers remain hesitant to share data, often citing time costs, risk of misuse, and limited personal benefit (Houtkoop et al., 2018; Abele-Brehm et al., 2019; Hendriks & Ramos, 2022; Gomes et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although acceptance of Open Science principles has increased (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Korbmacher et al., 2023)</ref>, some researchers remain hesitant to share data, often citing time costs, risk of misuse, and limited personal benefit <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Houtkoop et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abele-Brehm et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hendriks & Ramos, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Gomes et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the prospect of receiving citations and acknowledgements has been identified as one factor motivating researchers to share their data (Dorta-González et al., 2021; Wallis et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Indeed, the prospect of receiving citations and acknowledgements has been identified as one factor motivating researchers to share their data <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Dorta-González et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wallis et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The present results provide no evidence for a citation advantage associated with data sharing: the univariate FWCI difference did not persist after accounting for other article characteristics, and accumulated citation counts did not differ significantly by sharing status.
TOST equivalence was established for accumulated citations but not for FWCI, where an advantage of up to +38% remains compatible with the data.
Similarly, Bayes factors provided only weak support for the null hypotheses, leaving room for effects that this study did not have sufficient statistical power to resolve.
Several differences between data-sharing and non-sharing articles may help contextualize these results.
Data-sharing articles appeared in journals with higher twoyear mean citedness, were more likely to have an associated preprint, and tended to be more recent.
These characteristics could contribute to observed differences in citation impact, although their relationships with sharing status cannot establish the underlying mechanisms.
For example, journals with higher two-year mean citedness may be more likely to require data sharing, or researchers who share data may also be more likely to publish in such journals.
Similarly, preprints may increase an article's accessibility and opportunities to be cited.
The more recent publication dates of data-sharing articles are consistent with the increasing adoption of data-sharing practices, while also giving these articles less time to accumulate citations.
The temporal analysis further informs the differences in citation dynamics between sharing and non-sharing articles.
The significant interaction between sharing status and year post-publication corresponded to an estimated 4.5% annual decay in the citation ratio between the two groups.

Because prior studies (e.g., Colavizza et al., 2020; Piwowar et al., 2007) have reported substantial ODCA concentrated in the early postpublication period, I conducted exploratory analyses to examine whether a similar pattern was evident in the present sample.
text.formatted: Because prior studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Colavizza et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Piwowar et al., 2007)</ref> have reported substantial ODCA concentrated in the early postpublication period, I conducted exploratory analyses to examine whether a similar pattern was evident in the present sample.

text.text: Although unadjusted comparisons indicated higher citation counts for data-sharing articles in the first post-publication year, this difference was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for other article characteristics.
A comparison of cumulative citations over the first three postpublication years yielded a similar pattern.
Thus, despite the significant temporal interaction, these analyses did not establish an early ODCA.
Moreover, fewer articles contributed observations at longer publication lags, making estimates for later years less precise.
The temporal pattern is therefore best interpreted as evidence for a difference in citation trajectories, although its underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

The potential for secondary analysis is often cited as a key benefit of sharing research data (Martone et al., 2018; Weston et al., 2019). Godwin et al. (2025) argued that "the ideal raw data to facilitate new research are by-fixation datasets," which could potentially lead to a higher ODCA for articles sharing more granular data.
text.formatted: The potential for secondary analysis is often cited as a key benefit of sharing research data <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Martone et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Weston et al., 2019)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Godwin et al. (2025)</ref> argued that "the ideal raw data to facilitate new research are by-fixation datasets," which could potentially lead to a higher ODCA for articles sharing more granular data.

text.text: However, because large-scale bibliometric studies typically operationalize data sharing as a binary variable (e.g., Colavizza et al., 2020; Colavizza et al., 2024), it has remained unclear whether sharing finer-grained data is associated with greater citation impact.
text.formatted: However, because large-scale bibliometric studies typically operationalize data sharing as a binary variable (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Colavizza et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Colavizza et al., 2024)</ref>, it has remained unclear whether sharing finer-grained data is associated with greater citation impact.

text.text: In the present study, I found no evidence that finer-grained sharing was associated with a citation advantage over sharing coarser, aggregated data.
This finding suggests that the potential research benefits of granular data do not necessarily translate into greater citation impact, at least in the visual search and eye-movement literature.
It does not, however, indicate whether finer-grained data actually facilitate more secondary analyses, a benefit that citation-based measures cannot directly assess.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.

First, some article characteristics used in the analyses were imperfect proxies: venue two-year mean citedness served as a proxy for the proprietary Journal Impact Factor, and preprint availability depended on the identification of associated preprints.
Second, the analyses were observational and cannot establish causal relationships between data sharing and citation impact.
Unmeasured factors, such as research quality, topic prominence, or author reputation, may also contribute to the observed associations.
Third, the corpus was restricted to a relatively small, focused set of articles published between 2017 and 2022.
The sample size limited statistical power, particularly for analyses comparing granularity levels and for estimates at longer publication lags.
The findings may also not generalize to other research domains, or to current trends within the visual search literature.
Finally, citation counts and FWCI capture only one dimension of research impact and do not directly measure research quality, reproducibility, or the broader scientific value of shared data.

In sum, this study found no robust evidence that data sharing was associated with greater adjusted citation impact in visual search and eye-movement research, nor that sharing finer-grained data conferred an additional citation advantage.
The temporal interaction suggests that the association between sharing status and annual citation accrual may vary with time since publication, but its practical significance remains uncertain.

Data-sharing articles were also more likely to have associated preprints and appeared in journals with higher two-year mean citedness, although the direction and mechanisms of these relationships remain unclear.
Importantly, the analyses neither establish that data sharing provides no citation benefit nor rule out a modest advantage.
Advocates of Open Science should therefore be cautious about promoting data sharing on the promise of increased citation metrics alone.
Its potential contributions to secondary research, reproducibility, and scientific progress remain important reasons to support data sharing, even when citation benefits are uncertain.

In a recent publication,Pan et  al. (2026)examined the ODCA across 3,319 articles published between 2012 and 2016 in four prominent psychology journals.
They found that articles with publicly available data received approximately 20% more citations after adjusting for publication characteristics.
It remains unclear, however, whether this premium generalizes to specific research subfields.
Furthermore, because many largescale studies operationalize data sharing as a binary variable, it is not yet established whether the granularity of the shared data influences its citation impact.
In this study, I examine whether data sharing is associated with greater citation impact in visual search and eye-movement research.
To do so, I combined the Godwin et al. (2025) dataset with bibliometric indicators and article characteristics extracted from ).
